Campegius Vitringa
kam-pā'ji-us vi-tring'ga
n. (Campegius Vitringa the Elder, 1659–1722, professor at Franeker and expositor of Isaiah)
Latinized Campegius from the Frisian given name Kempo; Vitringa, a Frisian family name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Campegius Vitringa spent his life at Franeker in Friesland and produced the commentary on Isaiah that was the standard Reformed exposition of that prophet for a century and a half. It is a very large book, built on the Hebrew, careful with the history, and relentless in reading the prophet's promises as fulfilled in Christ and in the gospel church. He also wrote on the synagogue, on typology, and on the Revelation. Vitringa is the answer to anyone who imagines that the high orthodox period produced only systems: here is a man who gave decades to one prophet, line by line. What he was doing, our Lord did on the Emmaus road and in the synagogue at Nazareth: the prophets testify of him (Joh 5:39).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines prophecy as a foretelling, and exposition as a laying open the sense or meaning of a writing.

expand to see more

PROPH'ECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.

EXPOSI'TION, n. Explanation; interpretation; a laying open the sense or meaning of an author, or of any writing.

COM'MENTARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; a book of explanations or expositions.

SYN'AGOGUE, n. A congregation or assembly of Jews, met for the purpose of worship; the house appropriated to that worship.

Key Scripture

Joh 5:39 — "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me."

Luk 24:27 — "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself."

Isa 40:8 — "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever."

2Pe 1:20 — "Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation."

Modern Corruption

Decades on one prophet, line by line, and the standard Isaiah for a century and a half.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the historical-critical dismemberment of Isaiah into two or three authors separated by centuries, which the dictionary rejects: there is one prophet Isaiah, and the latter chapters are his. Vitringa read the book whole and read it as prophecy, which is why his exposition still has force and the nineteenth-century partition theories have mostly been abandoned even by their own successors.

The principle to recover is that prophecy is the Lord's word about his own Son and endures past every commentator. “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39). The permanence belongs to the word and not to the expositor: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). And no interpreter owns it: “no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” (2Pe 1:20).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word; Greek propheteia (G4394), prophecy, a word spoken for God.

expand to see more

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter, a thing spoken; Isaiah 40:8.

Hebrew nabel (H5034) — to fade, to wither, to droop; Isaiah 40:8.

Greek ereunao (G2045) — to search, to examine closely; John 5:39.

Greek propheteia (G4394) — prophecy, a word spoken for God; 2 Peter 1:20.

Greek diermeneuo (G1329) — to expound, to interpret fully; Luke 24:27.

Usage

"“they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39) — Isaiah read whole and read as prophecy."

"“the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — Franeker, and a very large book."

"“no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” (2Pe 1:20) — no interpreter owns it."
